stories.headline: A.P. seeks assistance from Tamil Nadu, Karnataka for cyclone power restoration
stories.title: A.P. seeks assistance from Tamil Nadu, Karnataka for cyclone power restoration
reasons: source: event has 3 copies, primary source counted once
corroboration: 2 independent source groups -> high confidence
article_sentences: Anticipating the possibility of large-scale damage to electricity infrastructure, particularly the uprooting of electric poles in cyclone-affected areas, Andhra Pradesh Chief Minister N Chandrababu Naidu on Sunday spoke with Tamil Nadu Chief Minister Vijay and Karnataka Chief Minister D.K. Shivakumar.
Naidu requested them to send necessary personnel and machinery to Andhra Pradesh to undertake electricity infrastructure restoration works in the wake of the cyclone.
Both Chief Ministers responded positively and assured they would extend all possible assistance to Andhra Pradesh.
Chandrababu Naidu said AP officials would coordinate with their counterparts in the two states to facilitate the required support.
Meanwhile, personnel from Telangana are already engaged in field-level operations to restore the electricity infrastructure damaged by Cyclone Arnab.

As a precautionary measure, the Andhra Pradesh Government has also kept electricity department personnel who have completed restoration work in Cyclone Arnab-affected areas ready for deployment in regions likely to be affected by Cyclone Murasu, the release added.

A scene at Marina Beach on November 1, 2026.
A deep depression over the Bay of Bengal on Sunday (November 1, 2026) intensified into a cyclone named “Murasu”.

stories.headline: Cyclone Murasu nears Andhra, Odisha days after Arnab; Chennai schools shut
stories.title: Cyclone Murasu nears Andhra, Odisha days after Arnab; Chennai schools shut
stories.summary: Cyclone Murasu nears Andhra, Odisha days after Arnab; Chennai schools shut
reasons: corroboration: single independent source -> medium confidence
article_sentences: Cyclone Murasu is approaching the Andhra Pradesh coast as authorities evacuate vulnerable residents.
The fresh threat has complicated ongoing relief operations after Cyclone Arnab.
Less than a week after Cyclone Arnab struck Andhra Pradesh, the state and neighbouring Odisha are preparing for another cyclone while relief and restoration work continues.
Cyclone Murasu is expected to cross the Andhra coast near Ongole late Monday night or early Tuesday, with winds of 100–110 kmph, gusting to 120 kmph.
Andhra Pradesh has deployed disaster response teams and ordered evacuations from unsafe areas.
Odisha is moving residents from low-lying settlements and landslide-prone hillsides, while Chennai has declared a school holiday on November 2 as heavy to very heavy rain is forecast.
The fresh threat comes as around 1.18 lakh people in Odisha remain affected by the floods and landslides following Arnab’s landfall on October 28.
Further rain in southern Odisha through November 4 could hamper recovery efforts and trigger fresh flooding and landslides.
Murasu intensified into a cyclonic storm over the Bay of Bengal on Sunday.

According to the India Meteorological Department’s (IMD) 5.30 pm update, it was about 420 kilometres east-southeast of Chennai and 490 kilometres east-southeast of Nellore, moving west-northwestwards at 25 kmph.
It is expected to strengthen into a severe cyclonic storm by the early hours of November 2 before turning northwestwards towards Andhra Pradesh.
The latest forecast places landfall between Nellore and Narsapur, close to Ongole in Prakasam district, between 11.30 pm on November 2 and 4 am on November 3.

stories.headline: US midterms: How Trump’s noncitizen voter lists could affect election results
stories.title: US midterms: How Trump’s noncitizen voter lists could affect election results
stories.summary: With Republicans fighting to retain control of Congress, the administration’s voter eligibility drive has raised questions over election challenges
reasons: corroboration: single independent source -> medium confidence
event term: 'election results' in title weight 64
article_sentences: As Americans head to the polls on Tuesday for midterm elections, lists the Trump administration has compiled of possible noncitizen voters could be used to contest the validity of the results.
With US President Donald Trump’s Republican Party fighting to maintain control of Congress, here’s how the lists could affect the midterms.

The Trump administration has acknowledged sending letters to election officials in five states — California, Washington, New Jersey, Pennsylvania and Nevada — as of October 30, saying it identified noncitizens on their voter rolls, according to a Justice Department document seen by Reuters.

In an October 13 letter, the Justice Department demanded California not count ballots from about 20,000 registered voters "who federal agencies reasonably believe are likely noncitizens" without first verifying their citizenship, warning that election workers who processed them could face prosecution.
Trump endorsed the warning on social media: “They will all go to jail for a long period of time!!!”
Noncitizen voting is illegal and can lead to jail time, fines and deportation.
The White House says noncitizen voting is a significant problem requiring aggressive enforcement to protect election integrity.
Trump has long alleged it is widespread, but available evidence indicates it is exceedingly rare.

A Reuters investigation in July found just 129 cases in which noncitizens were federally charged with voting illegally since a federal “voting by aliens” statute was created by Congress in 1996; many appeared to stem from confusion or administrative errors rather than intentional fraud.
The Justice Department has since ramped up noncitizens voting prosecutions.
“Close elections are not rare, and every illegal ballot cancels out the vote of an American citizen,” a Justice Department spokesperson, Kiersten Pels, said in a statement.
Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin claimed without evidence in a Fox News interview on Saturday that his agency had found 300,000 noncitizens on the voter rolls.

stories.headline: Jhelum is calling
stories.title: Jhelum is calling
stories.summary: River Jhelum, which is considered to be the lifeline of Kashmir, has been facing extreme ecological threat due to unabated pollution, illegal mining and encroachments. Jhelum serves a dual purpose for Kashmir—its major source for drinking water and irrigation and importantly saves the Valley from floods. Ironically the river has been fast losing both these functions in absence of conservation measures. Jhelum originates from Verinag in south Kashmir, spans over 175 sq Kms and settles in Wular lake before flowing to Pakistan Occupied Kashmir (PoK) from Baramulla district in north Kashmir. The river is propelled by four streams—Sundran, Brang, Arapath and Lidder is Anantnag district. Besides small streams like Veshav and Rambiara also fed the river with fresh lease of waters. All water bodies flow into Jhelum making it an important part of Kashmir’s interconnected hydrological system. Despite its immense ecological importance, Jhelum is facing extreme pollution as all drains from south to north Kashmir directly flow into the river. The irony is that instead of constructing Sewage Treatment Plants, authorities have set up hundreds of pumping stations to empty drains into the river. The problem is compounded by dumping of solid waste and illegal sand mining. All these factors have severely affected flora and fauna and the hydrological system of the river. Jhelum has lost its carrying capacity also. It has been observed that the river swells and overflows after incessant rains for even 2-3 days. Wetlands like Hokersar, Bemina, Narakara, Batamaloo numbal, Rakh-e-arth, Anchar and Gilsar on the left and right of Jhelum, which acted as reservoirs of floodwaters, have been encroached upon, filled and converted into colonies. Deterioration of these wetlands have affected their capacity to absorb flood water—putting extra pressure on Jhelum. Jhelum Action Plan formulated for four towns of Anantnag, Srinagar, Sopore and Baramulla to intercept, divert, transmit sewage of these areas and treat it in STPs is still on paper. The intervention of the High Court of Jammu and Kashmir to restore the glory of Jhelum is timely. A division bench comprising Chief Justice Dr Pushpendra Singh Bhati and Justice Yash Paul Bourney recently sought the report after Advocate Nadeem Qadiri, assisting as amicus curiae in the Public Interest Litigation (PIL) by Environmental Policy Group on conservation of Jhelum, raised concern over deteriorating condition of Jhelum. The Court has sought a report attesting to mining activities, proposed setting up of Sewage Treatment Plants (STPs) in river Jehlum as also construction or removal of embankments for flood control of the waterbody. It has also sought milestones achieved so far in the matter related to flood mitigation. EPG has filed the PIL in 2017 to flag the fragile flood management system in Kashmir and seek the court’s intervention for measures to protect Kashmir from future flood disasters. The PIL also highlights shortcomings in flood management due to which massive damage was caused during 2014 floods and seeks tangible steps to avoid such situations. EPG Convenor, Faiz Bakshi minces no words to raise red flags over illegal mining, untreated sewage discharge and condition of river embankments saying this has significant implications for the river’s ecological health, carrying capacity and flood-management system. EPG rightly states that these concerns cannot be addressed through administrative assurances alone and require transparent information, scientific assessment and effective implementation on the ground. Following incessant rains on September 7, 2014, Jhelum had crossed record 23-feet at Ram Munshi Bagh gauge, while level went over 36 feet at Sangam submerging localities on both sides of the river from south Kashmir to Srinagar. As per estimates flood water measuring about 120,000 cusecs surpassed the carrying capacity of Jhelum by five times. However no lessons have been learnt from the deluge. Despite the passage of 12 years, sustained and scientific measures are missing to increase the river’s carrying capacity. Believe it! Despite massive silt accumulation, no dredging has been undertaken in Jhelum in the last 5 years. On the other hand, unabated illegal mining in Jhelum’s tributaries —Doodh Ganga and Sukhnag has increased siltation in the river. An official report reveals that 15 lakh tonnes of riverbed material (RMB) comprising boulders, sand, nallah muck and gravel, were illegally extracted from Sukhnah river in the last several years. This wanton extraction of riverbed material severely altered the natural course of the river and extensively damaged its flora and fauna. Besides, imagine how many tons of silt must have been deposited in river Jhelum. The Ram Bagh flood spill channel looks like a forest with heavy growth of grass and other vegetation. Near Tengpora bridge, a vast chunk of the flood spill has been converted into a football ground. When water level in Jhelum rises, these bottlenecks hamper free flow of water. It is shocking to see how habitations have come up in the Jhelum’s floodplains. It was a practice of Dogra rulers to breach the Kandzal area to save Srinagar from floods. Excess water of Jhelum used to be diverted through Kandzal area and the waters would spread to Nowgam areas in central Kashmir Budgam areas. Now the Kandzal area is dotted with concrete constructions. The flood plains have been filled up! Earlier this year following incessant rains, Jhelum waters spread through its original flood plains from Shalina to Lasjan areas. The question is who allowed filling and constructions of Jhelum’s flood plains at the cost of endangering Srinagar city? Serious measures are missing to increase carrying capacity of Jhelum and restoration of its flood plains. We hope that judicial intervention will ensure long term conservation of Jhelum and restoration of its glory. And people shouldn’t forget that it’s also their responsibility to contribute their bit to protect their lifeline, the Jhelum. Author is Executive Editor, Greater Kashmir

stories.headline: J&K Draft Mountain Policy proposes visitor limits at tourist hotspots to check overcrowding
stories.title: J&K Draft Mountain Policy proposes visitor limits at tourist hotspots to check overcrowding
stories.summary: Srinagar, Nov 1: A draft policy on sustainable mountain development has proposed a major overhaul of tourism management, infrastructure development and environmental protection in Jammu and Kashmir, including daily visitor limits at popular destinations, restrictions on private vehicles, a green cess of up to Rs 2,000 for foreign tourists and tighter controls on construction in ecologically sensitive areas. The Draft Jammu and Kashmir Sustainable Mountain Development Policy (JK-SMDP 2026), dated October 12, 2026, envisages a framework to regulate tourism, protect fragile mountain ecosystems and ensure that local communities benefit from economic activity in the region. The document, which is still a draft for consideration, does not represent an approved government decision. Its recommendations would require formal approval and, where necessary, legal backing before they could be implemented. One of its key proposals is to introduce carrying-capacity limits at 15 high-pressure tourist destinations, including Gulmarg, Pahalgam, Sonamarg, Doodhpathri, Yusmarg, Gurez, Bangus, Sinthan Top, Patnitop, Katra, Paddar, Basoli and Bhaderwah. The draft proposes that scientific carrying-capacity studies be completed within 12 months. Pending these studies, interim daily visitor limits could be introduced within 100 days of the proposed policy’s approval, based on the capacity of roads, parking facilities and sanitation infrastructure. It also envisages an online registration and time-slot booking system for visitors at high-pressure destinations, supported by digital entry passes, cess collection, weather alerts and visitor data management. In a significant proposed change to tourist transportation, the draft recommends that private cars, taxis and buses be stopped at designated green gateways located approximately 10 kilometres below fragile destinations. Beyond these gateways, movement would be restricted to electric or CNG vehicles, walking, ponies or cycles. The document proposes that electric vehicle fleets be operated by local youth cooperatives, self-help groups and registered local operators, while outside operators would not be licensed. Tangmarg has been identified as a possible green gateway for Gulmarg, Pahalgam town for Aru, Betaab Valley and Chandanwari, and Sonamarg market for the Thajiwas area. Emergency, defence, disaster-response and essential local-service vehicles would be exempted. The draft also proposes a Mountain Green Cess, with different rates for domestic and foreign visitors. According to its detailed tariff table, domestic tourists would be charged Rs 500 at Zone B destinations, including Gulmarg, Pahalgam, Patnitop, Sonamarg and Doodhpathri, and Rs 1,000 at Zone A sites such as glaciers, high-altitude lakes, alpine meadows and high-altitude trekking routes. For foreign nationals, the proposed cess is Rs 2,000 at both categories of destinations. Children below 12 years, specially abled individuals and residents of the local body where a destination is situated have been proposed for exemption. Other Jammu and Kashmir residents and students on institutional tours would be charged Rs 100. The policy estimates that the cess could generate approximately Rs 750 crore annually, based on an estimated 1.5 crore to 2.5 crore tourists and a conservative average collection of Rs 500 per visitor. It proposes that the revenue be ring-fenced for destination-level environmental management, with 40 per cent allocated to waste collection, toilets and sanitation, 20 per cent to ecological restoration, 20 per cent to local employment, 10 per cent to visitor safety and rescue systems, and the remaining 10 per cent to monitoring and administration. The draft states: “Cess collected at a destination is spent at that destination; it cannot be diverted.” The document also proposes restrictions on new construction in high-risk and ecologically sensitive areas, including glacier forelands, stream corridors and identified hazard-prone zones. It calls for stronger land-use planning and environmental safeguards to prevent unregulated construction in mountain regions. On waste management, the draft envisages that every notified destination should be free of visible garbage and untreated sewage within three years. It proposes a ban on single-use plastics in notified destinations, deposit-refund mechanisms, material recovery facilities and a carry-in, carry-out system for visitors. Legacy waste at identified locations would be targeted for clearance within two years, while penalties would be introduced for violations. Disaster preparedness forms another major component of the proposed policy. It recommends multi-hazard risk mapping for hill towns, tourist destinations, pilgrimage routes and highways within three years, covering landslides, flash floods, avalanches, glacial lake outburst floods and earthquakes. It also proposes early-warning systems, trained community volunteers, rescue equipment and evacuation plans. The draft envisages automatic closure of tourist sites and routes during red alerts issued for extreme weather and other hazards. “We cannot stop cloudbursts, but we can stop them from becoming mass tragedies. The goal is zero avoidable deaths from mountain hazards,” the document states. Pilgrimage management has also been addressed, with the draft proposing science-based daily limits for yatras and religious destinations, including the Amarnath Yatra, Shri Mata Vaishno Devi, Machail Mata, Shiv Khori and Buddha Amarnath. It recommends temporary suspension of movement when weather and early-warning systems issue red alerts for cloudbursts, landslides or flash floods. The policy places considerable emphasis on creating employment opportunities for residents of mountain areas. It proposes local jobs in electric vehicle operations, waste management, recycling, guiding services, homestays, slope restoration and visitor assistance. “Protecting the mountains must put money in the pockets of mountain people. Regulation without livelihoods will fail; this Policy ties every rule to local jobs,” it states. For institutional implementation, the draft proposes a Jammu and Kashmir Mountain Development Authority and a non-lapsable J&K Mountain Green Fund. The proposed fund would receive money from the green cess, trekking and expedition fees, penalties, deposits and other sources, including government schemes, corporate social responsibility contributions and climate finance. The document also proposes that a J&K Sustainable Mountain Development Act be brought into law within one year, providing legal backing for inspections, penalties, restoration orders and enforcement measures. “A policy without legal teeth becomes a document on a shelf,” the draft states, adding that “This Policy shall move to law within one year.” The proposed implementation roadmap envisages action during the first 100 days following Cabinet approval, including the identification of three model destinations, interim visitor caps, pilot green gateways, cess collection and the launch of the proposed Mountain Pass platform. The draft proposes that scientific carrying-capacity studies be completed within 12 months.

Pending these studies, interim daily visitor limits could be introduced within 100 days of the proposed policy’s approval, based on the capacity of roads, parking facilities and sanitation infrastructure.

Beyond these gateways, movement would be restricted to electric or CNG vehicles, walking, ponies or cycles.
The document proposes that electric vehicle fleets be operated by local youth cooperatives, self-help groups and registered local operators, while outside operators would not be licensed.

Emergency, defence, disaster-response and essential local-service vehicles would be exempted.

stories.headline: One Health, One System
stories.title: One Health, One System
stories.summary: Many outbreaks that reach a hospital begin elsewhere, in wildlife or livestock, and cross into people through food, water or close contact. By the time the first case is diagnosed, the ecological event behind the outbreak may already be weeks old. That gap between the ecological event and the clinical diagnosis is the one that One Health, marked every year on November 3rd, is meant to close. The case for One Health rests on numbers that rarely change. The CDC and the World Organization for Animal Health (WOAH) estimate that about six in ten known human infectious diseases can spread between animals and humans, and roughly three in four new or emerging ones originate in animals. India is exposed by its own success. It is the world's largest milk producer and has one of the largest livestock populations, and its farms, forest fringes and informal markets bring people, animals and wildlife into constant contact. In such a landscape, the first sign of a human epidemic is often a pattern in animals that nobody connected: clustered abortions in cattle, unexplained deaths in a flock, a rise in fever cases at a primary health centre. Environmental change is steadily widening that exposure. Warmer, wetter conditions lengthen the breeding season and extend the range of insect vectors. Lumpy skin disease, caused by a capripoxvirus and spread by biting flies, mosquitoes and ticks, swept through Indian cattle in 2022 and has since reached many States, including Jammu and Kashmir. It does not infect people, yet it is a public health concern: it deprives households of milk, draught power and income, and these are the families least able to absorb the loss. Climate stress works through the food chain as well. Experimental work on elevated carbon dioxide has found lower nutrient composition in crops such as wheat and rice, while droughts and floods degrade fodder. Undernourished animals can be less productive and more susceptible to disease. More pests and fungi mean heavier pesticide use, and residues drain into rivers and aquatic food webs, returning the problem to human diets. Some risks reach us quietly, through the milk pail. Raw milk can carry bacteria such as Mycobacterium bovis, Brucella and Salmonella, which cause tuberculosis, brucellosis and salmonellosis in people. Brucellosis, for example, causes undulant fever, joint pain and fatigue, symptoms easily mistaken for typhoid or tuberculosis, so the disease is under-diagnosed and under-reported. Farmers and veterinarians carry occupational risk, and consumers carry the rest. Vaccinating female calves under the National Animal Disease Control Programme protects the herd, but it does not protect a household that receives unboiled milk from the unorganized sector. Pasteurization and the cold chain are therefore public health measures as much as dairy-economy ones. Antimicrobial resistance (AMR) is perhaps the clearest proof that the three domains are one. The Global Research on Antimicrobial Resistance study in The Lancet estimated 1.14 million deaths directly attributable to bacterial AMR in 2021 and projected nearly 39 million cumulative attributable deaths between 2025 and 2050. Antibiotics given to animals for growth promotion, prophylaxis or unsupervised treatment select for resistant bacteria and resistance genes. These pass through manure, water, soil and food to people, and then back to animals. India banned colistin, a last-resort antibiotic, in food-producing animals in 2019, and the Food Safety and Standards Authority of India has set residue limits. Enforcement, farm-level sales data and veterinary stewardship remain the weak links. The obstacle is institutional rather than scientific. Human disease surveillance sits with health authorities, animal disease reporting with animal husbandry departments, and wildlife and habitat data with forest and environment bodies. They rarely share a threshold for action, a database or a chain of command. Four global agencies, WHO, the Food and Agriculture Organization, WOAH and the UN Environment Programme, have drawn up a One Health Joint Plan of Action, but the real test is delivery in India’s districts. That begins with health, veterinary and environment teams meeting within hours of a suspected outbreak, guided by warning signs agreed in advance. It requires funded veterinary diagnostic laboratories linked to block-level dispensaries, with veterinarians treated as part of public health surveillance and not as a separate service. It requires a safer milk chain through pasteurisation and testing, antibiotics for animals sold only on prescription with sales recorded, and climate-linked surveillance of vectors and wildlife for early warning of outbreaks. Households can contribute too: boiling milk, cooking meat thoroughly, and washing produce are among the cheapest protections available. But the risk begins earlier, on the farm and in the environment. Protecting animals and the environment is part of protecting people. (The Author is a Veterinarian and an Independent Researcher. Email: dr.akhterrasool@rediffmail.com)
